description: Ore prospecting means reading the ground for metal-bearing rock: green and blue copper stains, rusty weathered caps called gossans, and heavy dark pebbles in stream gravels that may be tin ore. At Rudna Glava in Serbia, Vinča-culture miners followed copper veins by the fifth millennium BCE. Tin ore was scarcer and harder to recognise; its earliest sources are debated.

Cassiterite (tin ore) resists weathering
Vinca-culture miners at Rudna Glava followed copper veins by the fifth millennium BCE
Vinca-culture miners at Rudna Glava followed copper veins by the fifth millennium BCE

uncertainty: Dates for the earliest ore prospecting are inferred from mines and slag; Rudna Glava is usually placed in the fifth millennium BCE, but a recent study argues it was worked by at least the sixth [NGC-006]. Early tin working at Kestel-Goltepe (Taurus, about 3000 BCE) is disputed. Prospecting practices arose in many regions independently.

description: Stratigraphy reads rock layers as history. In 1669 Nicolaus Steno argued that sediments settle in horizontal layers, the lowest oldest. description: A controlled chain reaction keeps uranium fission steady: each splitting nucleus releases two or three neutrons, and on average one causes the next fission. uncertainty: Accounts of CP-1's start time and run duration differ [NUC-53]. The chain-reaction idea predates fission's discovery (Szilard, 1933).

description: Reprocessing dissolves spent reactor fuel in nitric acid and separates uranium and plutonium from fission products by solvent extraction, the PUREX method. Wartime separation chemistry worked out at Oak Ridge's X-10 was used at Hanford to extract weapons plutonium. Civil plants such as France's La Hague, operating since 1976, recycle plutonium into mixed-oxide fuel. The United States runs none.

description: Enrichment raises the share of fissile uranium-235 above its natural 0.7 per cent. Ore concentrate is first converted to uranium hexafluoride. Reactor fuel needs 3-5%, weapons far more, so the step is internationally safeguarded.

uncertainty: Centrifuge adoption was slowed by engineering difficulty; enrichment spread unevenly and remains one of the most restricted technologies.

description: Radioactive ore processing began with radium: in 1898 the Curies traced it through Joachimsthal pitchblende residues, and a Joachimsthal works held a radium monopoly in 1909-1913. Over half of today's uranium is dissolved underground in place; mill tailings stay radioactive.

description: Geophysical prospecting measures physical contrasts underground to find deposits with no surface trace. description: Nuclear physics studies the atom's tiny, dense nucleus, identified by Ernest Rutherford in 1911. Isotopes, the neutron (James Chadwick, 1932) and artificial radioactivity (1934) followed. In December 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium among products of neutron-irradiated uranium; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it as nuclear splitting, and Niels Bohr traced slow-neutron fission to uranium-235.

uncertainty: Meitner's exclusion from the 1944 Nobel Prize remains controversial [NUC-43]; Ida Noddack had suggested nuclear splitting in 1934 [NUC-40].

description: Radioisotopes can be made by bombarding stable atoms with particles.
